body:
What is a genetically modified organism?

A genetically modified organism (GMO) is an organism whose genetic material has been deliberately altered through biotechnology. The term is often used for organisms developed by genetic engineering rather than ordinary crossing and selection.

A transgenic organism contains genetic material introduced from another source through genetic engineering. A cisgenic organism receives genetic material from the same species or a sexually compatible species. A genome-edited organism may contain a targeted change without retaining newly introduced foreign DNA. These distinctions are scientifically useful, although regulatory definitions differ among countries.

Genetic modification may change an organism's resistance to insects, tolerance of environmental stress, nutritional properties or ability to produce a useful substance. The intended trait must be assessed in the actual organism; insertion of a gene does not guarantee the same performance in every environment.

Bt cotton: a major Indian example

Bt cotton is genetically engineered cotton that produces selected insecticidal proteins originating from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. The abbreviation Bt refers to the bacterium, not to a cotton variety or a chemical fertiliser.

The bacterium contains genes called cry genes, which encode particular Cry proteins. Selected cry genes have been introduced into cotton to provide protection against susceptible bollworm pests. Different Cry proteins act against different groups of insects, so the presence of a Bt trait does not mean protection from every agricultural pest.

How a Bt protein affects a susceptible insect

When a susceptible insect larva feeds on plant tissue containing an effective Bt protein, the protein can become active in the insect's gut and interact with specific gut cells. In susceptible insects, this damages the gut lining and can lead to the insect's death. The effect depends on the particular protein and the susceptibility of the insect.

Bt technology targets insect damage. It does not directly increase soil fertility, provide universal resistance to insects or guarantee higher yield in every field. Yield also depends on rainfall, soil, crop management, disease and other pests.

Why resistance management matters

If the same insect-control mechanism is relied upon repeatedly, individuals with greater tolerance can survive and reproduce. Over generations, the pest population may become less susceptible. This is called evolution of resistance.

Good agricultural management therefore involves monitoring pests and using suitable resistance-management practices. The relevant scientific principle is natural selection: the technology does not prevent susceptible and resistant insects from differing in survival.

India's commercial cultivation status

As of 5 November 2026, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee's published list identifies Bt cotton as India's only commercially approved genetically engineered crop for cultivation. Commercial cultivation approvals are distinct from permissions for confined research, field trials and development of genome-edited crop varieties under a different regulatory pathway.

Prelims focus

  • Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • cry genes encode selected insecticidal Cry proteins.
  • Bt cotton protects against susceptible bollworm pests, not all insects.
  • Resistance can evolve in pest populations through selection.
  • GEAC lists Bt cotton as India's only commercially approved GM crop for cultivation as of 5 November 2026.
  • Trap: Bt cotton is an insect-resistant crop; Bt does not stand for herbicide tolerance.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, chapter Biotechnology and its Applications, section 12.1, especially Bt cotton and Bt toxin (GPSC Books compendium vol. 35, PDF pp. 232–235); Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, Approved Products, Agriculture Applications—Commercially Approved, consulted 5 November 2026; GEAC, Biosafety Data of Approved GM Crops, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Bt cotton produces an insecticidal Cry protein that acts against susceptible bollworm larvae.

title: Genetically Modified Organisms and the Science of Bt Cotton

body:
Why genetically modified organisms are useful

Genetic engineering allows scientists to introduce or alter selected biological functions in plants, animals and microorganisms. A useful application begins with a desired characteristic, such as resistance to a particular pest or production of a human protein. Whether the modified organism delivers that benefit depends on its performance, safety and the conditions in which it is used.

Agricultural applications

Insect resistance and herbicide tolerance

Insect-resistant crops, such as Bt cotton, contain traits intended to protect them against particular insect pests. Herbicide-tolerant crops can survive application of certain herbicides that would otherwise damage the crop. These are different traits. A crop may contain one, both or neither.

Insect resistance may reduce damage from targeted pests and, in suitable circumstances, reduce the need for particular insecticide applications. Herbicide tolerance helps farmers control weeds but requires attention to herbicide use and the possible development of herbicide-resistant weeds.

Improving nutrition and stress tolerance

Biofortification aims to improve the nutritional value of food crops. Golden Rice is a genetically engineered rice developed to produce beta-carotene in the edible grain. Beta-carotene is a precursor of vitamin A. The example illustrates a nutritional objective; it does not establish that Golden Rice has permission for commercial cultivation in India.

Other research objectives include tolerance of salinity, drought or heat, improved storage characteristics and reduced crop losses. A useful laboratory trait must still be evaluated in the field.

Medical applications

Genetically engineered microorganisms can act as biological factories for medically important proteins. One well-known example is recombinant human insulin.

Human insulin is a protein hormone that helps regulate blood glucose. Recombinant DNA technology allows suitable host cells, including bacteria, to produce human insulin components or their precursors. The resulting product is processed and purified for medical use. This reduced dependence on insulin extracted from the pancreas of animals.

Recombinant microorganisms are also used to manufacture selected enzymes, therapeutic proteins and vaccine components. Such medicines must meet quality, safety and regulatory requirements. A product made through biotechnology is not automatically safer than every product made by another method.

Industrial applications

Microorganisms already play important roles in fermentation and food processing. Modern biotechnology can modify a microorganism to improve production of a particular enzyme or other useful substance. Examples include enzymes used in food processing and manufacturing.

A distinction is necessary: fermentation is not necessarily genetic engineering. Traditional curd, bread and other fermented products can be made using naturally occurring microorganisms. The use of a genetically engineered microorganism is an additional technological choice.

The organism used in production and the final product are not always the same thing. A purified protein manufactured by genetically engineered microbes does not necessarily contain living genetically engineered microbes.

Prelims focus

  • Bt cotton illustrates insect resistance.
  • Herbicide tolerance and insect resistance are different agricultural traits.
  • Golden Rice was developed to produce beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor.
  • Genetically engineered microorganisms can produce recombinant human insulin.
  • Traditional fermentation does not require genetic modification.
  • Trap: A purified biotechnology product need not contain the GMO used to manufacture it.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, chapter Biotechnology and its Applications, sections 12.1–12.2 (GPSC Books compendium vol. 35, PDF pp. 232–237); NCERT, Biology, Class XII, chapter Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, section 11.1 (compendium vol. 35, PDF pp. 218–220); Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, Approved Products, Agriculture Applications, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Modified crops gain useful traits; engineered microbes manufacture products that need not contain living GM microorganisms.
pictures.caption: A modified organism can produce a useful trait in a crop or manufacture a useful biological substance.

title: Agricultural, Medical and Industrial Applications of GMOs

body:
What biosafety means

Biosafety involves assessing and managing risks to human health, animals, plants and the environment arising from biological materials and biotechnology activities.

The assessment of a genetically modified organism must consider the organism, the introduced characteristic, its intended use and the conditions under which it may be released or consumed. The term GMO alone does not establish that an organism is either safe or harmful.

Environmental risks of GM crops

Gene flow

Gene flow is the movement of genetic material between populations. For example, pollen from a genetically modified crop may fertilise a compatible nearby plant. Whether this happens depends on biological compatibility, flowering time, distance and other conditions. Gene flow does not mean that a cotton plant can cross naturally with any unrelated plant species.

Effects on non-target organisms

A trait intended to affect one pest may need assessment for effects on other organisms, such as beneficial insects or organisms involved in the wider ecosystem. These effects depend on the particular trait and exposure conditions; they cannot be assumed to be identical for all GM crops.

Development of resistance

If an insect population is repeatedly exposed to the same insecticidal trait, individuals with inherited resistance may survive and reproduce. Likewise, repeated use of a herbicide may favour resistant weeds. This creates an agricultural management problem even if the technology initially works effectively.

Biodiversity and farming practices

Large-scale cultivation of any crop may influence biodiversity, especially when associated with monoculture or changes in pesticide use. A sound assessment distinguishes the effects of the introduced genetic trait from the effects of farming practices more generally.

Food safety and allergenicity

Food safety assessment may examine nutritional composition, potential toxicity, allergenicity and changes associated with the intended modification. Allergenicity means the capacity of a substance to cause an allergic reaction in susceptible individuals. A newly expressed protein may require evaluation for possible allergenic effects.

Safety cannot be decided merely by asking whether a gene came from a different organism. The relevant questions are what substance is produced, how much is produced, whether people may be exposed to it and what scientific evidence shows about its effects.

Why labelling and traceability matter

Labelling provides information about a food product. Traceability helps identify a product's origin and movement through the supply chain. These can support consumer choice, monitoring and recalls where necessary.

Labelling requirements differ across jurisdictions and depend on the legally applicable rules. India's Food Safety and Standards Authority of India published draft Genetically Modified Foods Regulations in 2022. A draft proposal must not be treated as an enforceable final regulation merely because it was published. Food approvals and any applicable labelling requirements must be assessed under the rules in force.

Food safety concerns effects of consumption. Environmental biosafety concerns effects of cultivation, release and interaction with ecosystems. The same organism can require both kinds of assessment.

Prelims focus

  • Gene flow is the movement of genetic material between populations.
  • Compatible plants are needed for gene flow through normal cross-pollination.
  • Resistance may develop through natural selection in insects or weeds.
  • Food assessment can include toxicity, allergenicity and nutritional composition.
  • Labelling and traceability serve different but related purposes.
  • Trap: A draft regulation is not automatically an enforceable law.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, chapter Biotechnology and its Applications, sections 12.1 and 12.4 (GPSC Books compendium vol. 35, PDF pp. 232–239); Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, Biosafety Data of Approved GM Crops, sections on toxicity and allergenicity, consulted 5 November 2026; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, Draft Food Safety and Standards (Genetically Modified Foods) Regulations, 2022, chapters I and labelling provisions, published 21 November 2022.]

pictures.alt: Four possible pathways connect GM crop cultivation to gene flow, non-target exposure, resistance and biodiversity effects.
pictures.caption: Environmental assessment considers gene flow, non-target organisms and the evolution of resistance.

title: Biosafety, Environmental Risks and Food Labelling

body:
The legal foundation

India regulates activities involving genetically engineered organisms through a framework that includes the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Microorganisms, Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989, commonly called the 1989 Rules.

The 1989 Rules provide a system of biosafety oversight for research, handling and environmental release. They establish or recognise committees with different responsibilities. Permission for laboratory research is not the same as permission for commercial cultivation or general environmental release.

Important regulatory bodies

BodyFull nameMain responsibility
RDACRecombinant DNA Advisory CommitteeAdvises on developments, policies and safety regulations
IBSCInstitutional Biosafety CommitteeInstitution-level biosafety oversight and compliance
RCGMReview Committee on Genetic ManipulationResearch-related safety review under the Department of Biotechnology
GEACGenetic Engineering Appraisal CommitteeAppraises environmental release and large-scale activities from the environmental perspective
SBCCState Biotechnology Coordination CommitteeState-level monitoring, inspection and response
DLCDistrict Level CommitteeDistrict-level monitoring of relevant activities and compliance

Distinguishing the important committees

The IBSC operates at the institution handling genetically engineered organisms. It helps implement biosafety guidelines and serves as a point of contact for regulatory requirements.

The RCGM functions under the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science and Technology. It monitors safety aspects of ongoing research and related activities involving genetically engineered organisms and cells.

The GEAC functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). It appraises proposals for environmental release of genetically engineered organisms and products, including relevant experimental field trials, and examines large-scale activities from the environmental perspective.

The SBCC and DLC perform monitoring functions at state and district levels, respectively. They do not replace the national-level regulatory functions of RCGM and GEAC.

Why GEAC has two commonly encountered names

GEAC was formerly known as the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee. Its name was changed to Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee through a notification dated 16 July 2010. Both names may appear in older study materials, but Appraisal is the revised name.

Regulatory review is not a single permission covering every stage of development. Research oversight, confined trials, environmental release, product safety and commercial use can involve different requirements and authorities.

Prelims focus

  • The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in 1986.
  • The principal Indian rules for hazardous microorganisms and genetically engineered organisms were notified in 1989.
  • RCGM functions under the Department of Biotechnology.
  • GEAC functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
  • GEAC's present expansion is Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee; the name changed in 2010.
  • Trap: IBSC oversight of research does not by itself authorise commercial environmental release.

[Sources: Department of Biotechnology, RCGM Secretariat, Committees under the 1989 Rules, sections RDAC, IBSC, RCGM, GEAC, SBCC and DLC, consulted 5 November 2026; Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, Functions, consulted 5 November 2026; Department of Biotechnology, RCGM Secretariat, GEAC entry noting the 16 July 2010 name-change notification.]

pictures.alt: India's biosafety bodies: RDAC advises, IBSC oversees institutions, RCGM reviews research, GEAC appraises release, and SBCC and DLC monitor locally.
pictures.caption: India's biotechnology oversight system assigns different responsibilities to institutional, research, environmental and local bodies.

title: India's Regulatory Framework for Genetically Engineered Organisms
